To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the effects of experience with visual stimuli on the selectivity of the high-level ventral visual pathway depend on the task contexts in which the experience occurs, and (2) the effects of such experience transfer to novel objects that are similar in parts to the objects used during learning.

1) the effects of perceptual experience in the visual cortex depend on task context; 2) the effects of task context on visual cortex selectivity are specific to the task; and 3) the effects of training are transferred to novel objects.
The functional properties of the visual word form (VWFA), a high-level perceptual region in the visual word form cortex, can be shaped by the experience with visual stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural bases of the perception of objects and faces.
the role of top-down influences (task context) in learning to perceive objects and the nature of object representations that are formed during learning.
how the human brain learns to process objects and how this learning process is affected by top-down task context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

experience with novel stimuli produces a greater change in selectivity of the VWFA when the stimuli are associated with a meaningful context but produces a greater change when trained in a nonmeaningful context.
the effect of experience on the high-level visual areas depends on both bottom-up stimulus information and top-down task context.
the effects of experience are modulated by top-down influences and that these influences are determined by the way objects are processed during the learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of experience depend on both the stimulus information and task context in which experience occurs, and that the effect of experience on high-level perceptual areas is not limited to the specific trained objects.
top-down influences on learning to perceive objects are important, and they can be manipulated to facilitate learning.
learning is transferred from the trained objects to novel objects that have similar parts with the trained object.
The main takeaway from our work is that
top-down task context modulates the effect of experience on functional selectivity of the high-level cortex.
top-down task context can modulate the effects of experience and learning on the functional properties of high-level visual cortex in humans.
the effects of experience in shaping the high-level visual system depend not only on bottom-up stimulus information but also on top-down task context.
